1A-TZ1: A1
Instantaneous velocity
Instantaneous velocity is the rate of change of position at an instant: v = dx/dt. Displacement divided by a finite time interval gives average velocity; distance-based expressions describe speed.
A1
Acceleration–time graph and final speed
The change in velocity is the signed area under the acceleration–time graph. The object starts from rest, so summing the areas up to 8.0 s gives its final speed, 32 m s⁻¹.
A2
Resolving the force on an accelerating cube

Resolve the applied force along the vertical. Its upward component is F cos θ and the weight is mg downward. Newton’s second law gives a = (F cos θ − mg)/m. The frictionless surface supplies a horizontal normal reaction.
A2
Buoyancy and displaced volume

For a fully submerged object, buoyancy is the weight of displaced water: F = ρ_water gV. Halving the radius reduces the volume by a factor of eight. The sphere’s own density does not change this displaced volume, so F₁/F₂ = 8.
A2
Angular velocity of an orbiting satellite
One orbit is 2π radians and 24 h is 86400 s. Thus ω = 2π/T = 2π/86400 ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹.
A2
Impulse and final kinetic energy
Impulse equals the change in momentum. Starting from rest, p = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹. Then E_k = p²/(2m) = 2.0²/(2 × 5.0) = 0.40 J.
A3
A4
Angular acceleration and angular momentum
Four rotations give an angular displacement of 8π radians. Using ω² = 2αθ from rest gives ω = 4√(πα). Since L = Iω, the change in angular momentum is 4I√(πα).
A4
Moment of inertia of two spheres
Each 10 kg sphere is 4.0 m from the axis. Treating them as small particles, I = Σmr² = 2 × 10 × 4.0² = 320 kg m². The connecting rod has negligible mass.
A5
Relativistic addition of velocities

Use relativistic velocity addition rather than adding speeds directly. With the spacecraft moving at +0.50c in X and −0.50c in Y, the relative speed of the observers is (0.50c + 0.50c)/(1 + 0.50 × 0.50) = 0.80c.
B1
Melting ice with warm water
The water cools to 0 °C and releases mcT. This energy melts ice at its melting point, requiring m_melt L. Equating the energies gives m_melt = mcT/L.
B2
Cause of the enhanced greenhouse effect

Burning fossil fuels increases atmospheric greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide. These gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation and alter Earth’s energy balance. The supplied mark scheme selects burning fossil fuels.
B4
Rapid compression of an ideal gas

Rapid compression leaves little time for heat transfer. The moving piston does work on the gas; collisions with it increase molecular kinetic energy and therefore the molecules’ average speed. Compression itself is not thermal energy transfer.
B3
B4
Recognising a Carnot cycle

A Carnot cycle consists of two reversible isothermal processes joined by two reversible adiabatic processes. On a P–V diagram the adiabats are steeper than the isotherms. Identify the diagram with this pair of each type; the official key selects C.
B5
Equivalent resistance in three circuits
Reduce each network using the series and parallel rules. The combinations give their smallest equivalent resistance for Q, then R, then P. This is the ordering Q, R, P in the supplied key.
B5
Current produced by a charged moving belt
In one second the belt carries an area wv past the contact. Current is charge per second, I = σwv = (5.0 × 10⁻³)(0.60)(2.5) = 7.5 × 10⁻³ A = 7.5 mA.
B5
Resistance after reshaping a conductor
The material and volume stay constant. Increasing the length by a factor of four reduces the cross-sectional area by four. From R = ρL/A, resistance increases by 4 × 4 = 16, from 50 Ω to 800 Ω.
C1
Two springs connected in parallel
Identical springs in parallel have an effective spring constant 2k. Since T = 2π√(m/k), keeping the same mass gives T₂/T₁ = 1/√2.
C2
Reading period and amplitude from a wave graph
The amplitude is the largest displacement from equilibrium, 5.0 nm, not the peak-to-peak displacement. The period is 4.0 ms, so f = 1/T = 250 Hz.
C1
Speed at a specified displacement in SHM
The distance between the turning points is b, so A = b/2. Halfway from equilibrium to a turning point, x = A/2. Use v = ω√(A² − x²) with ω = 2πf to obtain v = (√3/2)πfb.
C3
Refraction through parallel layers
Measure angles from the normal. The 50° angle to the surface corresponds to 40° to the normal. Snell’s law gives (5/3)sin 40° = (4/3)sin θ, so θ ≈ 53°.
C3
Double-slit fringes and the diffraction envelope

At small angles, the interference-fringe spacing is approximately λ/d and the first diffraction minimum is at λ/b. Reading these two angular scales separately from the graph gives λ/d = 0.01 and λ/b = 0.1.
C4
Fifth harmonic in a pipe closed at one end
For a pipe closed at one end, the allowed harmonics are odd and L = nλ/4. At the fifth harmonic, λ = 4L/5.
C3
Number of maxima from a diffraction grating
The slit separation is d = 1/(400000) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m. With d sin θ = nλ and sin θ ≤ 1, the maximum order is 4. Count four maxima on each side plus the central maximum: 9.
D1
Comparing gravitational fields at planetary surfaces
Surface gravity is proportional to M/R². The smaller planet has mass M_E/18 and radius R_E/3, so g_P/g_E = (1/18)/(1/9) = 1/2.
D1
Gravitational potential above Earth’s surface

Outside Earth, V = −GM/(R + d), taking zero potential at infinity. At d = 0 the potential is finite and negative; as d increases it approaches zero from below with a decreasing positive gradient. This corresponds to A.
D2
Fundamental units of μ₀ε₀
The electromagnetic wave relation is c² = 1/(μ₀ε₀). Therefore μ₀ε₀ has units 1/c² = s² m⁻², expressed in fundamental SI units.
D2
Electric field from a potential gradient
The magnitude of a uniform electric field is the potential change divided by separation. Convert 20 kV to 20000 V and 5.0 cm to 0.050 m: E = 20000/0.050 = 4.0 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹.
D3
Magnetic field from the force on a current-carrying wire
For a perpendicular wire, F = BIL. Use the changes: B = ΔF/(LΔI) = (4.0 × 10⁻³)/(0.32 × 5.0) = 2.5 × 10⁻³ T = 2.5 mT.
D3
Magnetic forces on a current loop

Conventional current is opposite to the motion of negative charge carriers. Applying F = IL × B around the loop gives radial outward forces, so the loop’s diameter tends to increase. There is no net torque rotating it in its own plane.
E1
Evidence that electric charge is quantised
Millikan’s oil-drop experiment measured charges that were integer multiples of a common smallest charge. This established experimental evidence for quantisation of electric charge.
D4
Changing the speed of an AC generator

For a rotating coil, the peak emf is proportional to angular speed and the period is inversely proportional to it. Reducing the speed to 3/4 of the original reduces 10 V to 7.5 V and multiplies the original period by 4/3, giving about 1.1 ms.
E1
Nuclear notation for an ion
The atomic number is the number of protons, 53. The mass number is protons plus neutrons, 53 + 89 = 142. Changing the number of electrons changes the ionic charge but not the nuclear notation.
E1
Nuclear density and nucleon number

Nuclear mass is approximately proportional to nucleon number A, while nuclear radius is proportional to A^(1/3). Volume is therefore proportional to A as well, giving an approximately constant nuclear density.
E2
Maximum speed of a photoelectron
The photoelectric equation gives maximum kinetic energy E − Φ. Set ½m_e v_max² = E − Φ and solve: v_max = √[2(E − Φ)/m_e].
E2
Changes to a photon in Compton scattering

In Compton scattering the photon transfers energy to the electron, so its wavelength increases and λ/λ₀ > 1. Every photon in vacuum obeys λf = c, before and after scattering. Therefore (λf)/(λ₀f₀) = 1, giving option A.
E3
Deflection of radioactive emissions
Alpha and beta particles carry electric charge, so both electric and magnetic fields can deflect them. Gamma photons are uncharged, so they are not deflected by these fields.
E3
Decay sequence that produces an isotope

An isotope must retain the same proton number. One alpha decay lowers the proton number by 2 and mass number by 4; two beta-minus decays raise the proton number by 2 in total. The final proton number is restored but the mass number differs.
E4
Choosing a nuclear reactor moderator
A moderator slows fast neutrons through collisions while absorbing relatively few of them. Water is a suitable moderator. Control-rod materials instead absorb neutrons to regulate the chain reaction.
E4
Neutron balance in a steady chain reaction

For a steady chain reaction, exactly one of the four emitted neutrons per fission must cause the next fission on average. Thus three must be absorbed or lost: N_c + N_l = 3. Of the listed pairs, 2 and 1 satisfy this condition.
E5
Distance from a stellar parallax angle
Using parallax in arc-seconds, distance in parsecs is d = 1/p. For p = 1 × 10⁻² arc-second, d = 100 pc.
1A-TZ2: A1
Initial speed of a ball thrown upwards
Take upwards as positive: the displacement is −50 m, the acceleration is −g and time is 5.0 s. From s = ut + ½at², u = [−50 + ½g(5.0)²]/5.0 ≈ 15 m s⁻¹.
A1
Displacement in successive seconds

The acceleration is constant and the object starts from rest, so displacement is proportional to t². The total displacement after two seconds is 4 × 1.5 = 6.0 m. During the second second alone it is 6.0 − 1.5 = 4.5 m.
A2
Effect of air resistance on projectile motion

Air resistance reduces the maximum height and the horizontal velocity. At the highest point the velocity, and therefore drag, is horizontal, so the vertical acceleration remains g downward. The reduced horizontal motion also makes the impact direction steeper. All three statements are correct.
A1
A2
Free-body diagram on a banked road

Weight acts vertically downwards and the normal reaction is perpendicular to the road. At the maximum speed, the tendency is to slip up the bank, so friction acts down the slope. The diagram satisfying all three directions is D.
A2
Terminal speed and the radius of a sphere

For Stokes flow, drag is proportional to rv, while weight minus upthrust is proportional to r³ for the same materials. Balancing forces at terminal speed gives v_t proportional to r². Doubling the radius gives 4v.
A4
Number of revolutions of an accelerating wheel
For constant angular acceleration from rest, the mean angular velocity is half the final value. Angular displacement is ½(5π)(4.0) = 10π radians, or 5 complete revolutions.
A4
Units of angular impulse
Angular impulse is torque multiplied by time, or the change in angular momentum. Its SI unit is N m s, equivalent to kg m² s⁻¹.
A4
Rotational and translational energy of a moving car
Each wheel has rotational energy ½Iω² = ¼mv² because I = ½mR² and ω = v/R. Four wheels therefore have total rotational energy mv². Divide by the car’s translational energy ½Mv² to obtain 2m/M.
B1
Power radiated by two black bodies
Black-body power is proportional to R²T⁴. Since T_X = 2T_Y and P_Y = 2P_X, R_Y² = 2 × 16R² = 32R². Thus R_Y = 4√2 R.
B2
Incoming solar intensity and albedo
An albedo of 0.25 reflects one quarter of the incoming radiation. The remaining intensity is (1 − 0.25)S = 3S/4. The Sun is directly overhead here; the global-average factor of 1/4 does not apply.
B3
Pressure and density of gases at the same temperature

For an ideal gas, P = Nk_BT/V. Equal numbers of molecules in equal volumes at equal temperatures give equal pressures. More massive molecules give more mass in the same volume, so the densities differ.
B4
Identifying an isothermal stage on a P–V cycle

The isothermal curve is less steep than an adiabat through the same region. Compression during the isothermal stage means volume decreases along Z. Following the rest of the cycle then gives the clockwise direction, option D.
B5
Heating power and wire length

Use R = V²/P. The first wire has resistance 200²/500 = 80 Ω and the second has resistance 400²/2000 = 80 Ω. Same material and cross-section mean R is proportional to length, so the second length is L.
B5
Current ratio in a resistor network

Let the potential difference across the whole network be V and each resistance be R. The top branch contains only X, so I_X = V/R. The bottom branch has R in series with two parallel resistors, giving R + R/2 = 3R/2. Its current is 2V/(3R), which splits equally, so I_Y = V/(3R). Therefore I_X/I_Y = 3, option D.
C1
Acceleration–displacement graph for SHM
Simple harmonic motion satisfies a = −ω²x. The acceleration–displacement graph is therefore a straight line through the origin with negative gradient.
C1
Maximum elastic potential energy in SHM
The largest spring energy is E_max = ½kA². Doubling the amplitude quadruples it; changing the mass does not change this expression for the same spring. The new value is 4E.
C2
Average particle speed in a transverse wave

In a complete oscillation a particle travels a total distance 4A. The graph gives A = 4.0 cm and T = 20 ms, so its average speed is 4(0.040)/0.020 = 8 m s⁻¹. Transverse particle motion is perpendicular to wave travel.
C2
Frequency and nature of ultraviolet radiation
Ultraviolet radiation is an electromagnetic wave and is transverse. Its frequency is of order 10¹⁵ Hz. A value around 10⁻⁷ is a possible wavelength in metres, not a frequency in hertz.
C4
Phase in a fifth-harmonic standing wave

For a pipe closed at both ends, the fifth harmonic has displacement nodes every L/5 = 5 cm. Points in neighbouring loops oscillate in antiphase. The positions 2 cm and 7 cm are in adjacent loops and differ in phase by π.
C1
Lightly damped oscillations

For a fixed lightly damped system, amplitude gradually decays but the oscillation frequency remains constant in time. Its damped frequency is slightly below the undamped natural frequency, so exact equality is not the correct statement.
D1
Speed of a planet in a circular orbit
For an orbit around the same star, v = √(GM_star/r), independent of the planet’s own mass. Increasing the orbital radius to 1.5R gives v₂/v₁ = √(1/1.5) = √(2/3).
D2
Resultant electric field between two positive charges
The two fields at P point in opposite directions. Apply E = kQ/r² to each charge using the distances shown, then subtract. The resultant magnitude is kQ/(2x²), directed to the right.
D2
Magnetic field lines between like poles

Outside a bar magnet, field lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole. They do not cross or connect one north pole to another. The field lines between the facing north poles curve away from the central region; diagram C obeys these rules.
D3
Electric field and proton kinetic energy
The potential difference is 450 − 200 = 250 V across 0.50 m, so E = 500 N C⁻¹. A proton moving to the higher potential gains electrical potential energy, so its kinetic energy decreases.
D2
D3
Identifying particles from magnetic deflection

Use the magnetic-force direction for positive and negative charges. The undeflected path is the neutron. The two oppositely curved paths are the proton and electron, giving Q: proton, R: neutron, S: electron.
D3
Force on a movable current-carrying rod

For the rod to move right with the field directed out of the page, the conventional current through the rod must be upward. This is an anti-clockwise current around the circuit. The wire is perpendicular to the field, so the initial force is BIL sin 90°.
D2
Force between two parallel current-carrying wires

Force per unit length is proportional to I_X I_Y/r. Doubling one current and doubling the separation cancel. Reversing both currents preserves their opposite directions, so the force remains repulsive with magnitude F.
D4
Magnetic field from an induced average emf
A 180° rotation changes the flux from BA to −BA, so the magnitude of the flux change is 2BA. From ε_avg = 2BA/Δt, B = (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(2.0)/[2(4.0 × 10⁻⁴)] = 5.0 mT.
D4
Coil rotation and the induced emf graph

An emf is induced only when the rotation changes magnetic flux through the coil. Rotation about the field direction does not do that. The orientation and quarter-cycle variation shown correspond to a π/2 rotation about XX′, option A.
D4
Effect of smaller oscillation amplitude on induced current

The period of the mass–spring motion does not depend on amplitude in the SHM model. A smaller amplitude reduces the magnet’s speed and the rate of flux change, reducing the induced-current amplitude while retaining the period. The matching trace is D.
C1
B3
Masses of equal-volume gas samples
Equal P, V, and T imply equal numbers of molecules. Compare molecular masses using the given nuclides: CH₄ = 16, H₂O = 18, and CO₂ and N₂O = 44. Methane therefore has the smallest mass.
E1
E1
Longest-wavelength photon from atomic transitions
For an emitted photon, E = hc/λ. The longest wavelength corresponds to the smallest downward energy change. In the given energy-level diagram this is transition E₄.
E1
Distance of closest approach in Rutherford scattering
An alpha particle accelerated through V gains kinetic energy 2eV. At closest approach to gold this equals k(2e)(79e)/r. Cancelling 2e gives r = 79ke/V, with V = 7.7 × 10⁶ V.
E2
Work functions from photoelectric graphs

In E_k,max = hf − Φ, the frequency-axis intercept is the threshold frequency Φ/h. Surface Y has the larger threshold frequency in the graph, so it has the larger work function. Intensity does not set the threshold frequency.
E2
Radiation intensity and photon arrival rate
Intensity is photon arrival rate per unit area multiplied by energy per photon. Doubling wavelength halves hc/λ, while doubling the arrival rate cancels that change. The intensity remains I.
E5
Fusion and fission energy per unit fuel mass
Energy released is proportional to the mass defect. Compare per unit fuel mass: (0.024/5)/(0.48/235) = 2.35. This is different from comparing energy per single reaction.
E4
E3
Properties of gamma radiation
Gamma photons travel at c in a vacuum, faster than massive beta particles, and are more penetrating. Their ionising ability is lower, not greater. Thus statements I and II are correct.
E3
Decay constant from sample mass and activity
Find the number of nuclei using N = (4.4/222)N_A ≈ 1.19 × 10²². Activity is A = λN, so λ = (2.5 × 10¹⁶)/N ≈ 2.1 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹.
E4
Role of a moderator in a nuclear reactor

The moderator reduces neutrons’ kinetic energy through collisions, increasing the chance of thermal-neutron-induced fission. It is distinct from control rods, which absorb neutrons, and the coolant, which transports energy.
E5
Stellar radius from apparent brightness
For equal surface temperatures, apparent brightness is proportional to R²/d². Star Y is at half the distance and twice as bright, so 4R_Y²/R² = 2. Therefore R_Y = R/√2.

Compare field uniformity over the length of the magnetic needle, not just the field at the centre. 1B-TZ2: Resistivity of a wire and propagated measurement uncertainty

Reject the anomalous diameter reading with a justified reason before finding the mean. Use ρ = RA/L with A = πd²/4. In percentage uncertainty, the diameter contribution is doubled because area depends on d²; combine it with the resistance and length contributions as the scheme specifies.
Testing the ideal-gas relationship using a graph

Work, force–distance graphs and car motion

Area under a force–distance graph is work done. Relate the net work to the change in kinetic energy and use the force balance or power relation for the later motion. Retain units and distinguish instantaneous graph values from integrated areas.

D1
Orbital motion of Venus and gravitational relationships

For a near-circular orbit use v = 2πr/T and GM/r² = v²/r. These combine into the period–radius relationship. Convert all times and lengths to SI units before substituting, and follow the official scheme for the required derived quantities.

Rutherford scattering, nuclear structure and gamma photons

Use energy conservation to relate an alpha particle’s initial kinetic energy to its electrical potential energy at closest approach. For gamma transitions, photon energy is hf and corresponds to the change in nuclear energy. The supplied marking points specify the required nuclear interpretations.

B4
Microstates, entropy and energy distributions

Count the ways distinguishable particles can occupy each energy distribution, rather than counting only the drawn energy levels. The more probable macrostate has the greater number of microstates. Connect entropy to the multiplicity using S = k_B ln Ω where required.
C5
Doppler effect and the frequency of detected sound

A lower detected frequency means the detector moves away from the stationary source. Use the moving-observer Doppler relation with consistent signs. The source wavelength in the air is set by the sound speed and source frequency, independently of the detector’s motion.

D3
Acceleration and deflection of an electron in electric fields

First use eV = ½m_e v² for the accelerating potential. Resolve the later motion into an unchanged component and a component accelerated by the electric force. Use the time spent between the plates to calculate the displacement and subsequent trajectory.

A5
Spacetime intervals and simultaneity in different frames

Read coordinates from the spacetime diagram and evaluate the invariant interval using a consistent sign convention. Events that are simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another. Use the geometry of the tilted axes or Lorentz transformations as required.

Earth’s radiation balance, solar fusion and stellar evolution

For Earth’s energy balance distinguish the solar constant from the average over a sphere, apply albedo, and use emitted power per area proportional to T⁴. 2-TZ2: Elastic collision of carts and impulse

Check both momentum conservation and kinetic energies before and after the collision to establish elasticity. The average force follows from impulse divided by collision duration. Use the velocity–time information consistently for each cart.
Thermal conduction, heating and thermodynamic energy changes

Conduction transfers internal energy through interactions between particles and, in metals, mobile electrons. Use the temperature gradient and thermal conductivity for the rate of energy transfer. Apply the first and second laws carefully to the later heating and cooling situations.
Alpha-particle motion between electric and magnetic fields

For the plates use E = ΔV/d and electric force qE with the alpha particle’s charge +2e. Find acceleration and motion using its mass. When a magnetic field is introduced, use the vector direction and magnitude of qv × B and compare it with the electric force.
